knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(ggplot2)

# Part 1: Reproducible workflow

This document combines code, output and interpretation. The data file
`COSC_423_Results.csv` sits in the same folder as this `.Rmd`, so it can be
re-knitted on any machine.

## Load and tidy the data

The sheet has three header rows (title, maximum marks, column names) and two
columns both called "Total" (attendance and final mark), so I skip the header
rows and name the 47 columns myself.

```{r load}
col_names <- c("id", paste0("att_", 1:20), "att_total", "att_marks", "att_pct",
               "gender", "cgpa_range", "att_score", paste0("q", 1:6), "quiz",
               "a1", "a2", "assignments", "mid_sem", "ca", "python_lab", "r_lab",
               "exam_raw", "exam_30", "main_exam", "total_score", "grade",
               "pass_fail")

results <- read.csv("COSC_423_Results.csv", skip = 3, header = FALSE,
                    col.names = col_names, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
results <- results[grepl("^CSA", results$id), ]
results$pass_fail <- factor(results$pass_fail)
results$gender <- factor(results$gender)

head(results[, c("id", "gender", "cgpa_range", "ca", "main_exam",
                 "total_score", "grade", "pass_fail")])
dim(results)
str(results[, c("id", "gender", "ca", "main_exam", "total_score", "grade")])
```

```{r missing}
sum(is.na(results$total_score))
```

There are `r nrow(results)` students and `r sum(is.na(results$total_score))`
missing final scores. The analysis uses `total_score` (the final mark out of
100).

# Part 2: Descriptive statistics

```{r descriptives}
scores <- results$total_score

mean_score   <- mean(scores, na.rm = TRUE)
median_score <- median(scores, na.rm = TRUE)
mode_score   <- as.numeric(names(sort(table(scores), decreasing = TRUE)[1]))

var_score   <- var(scores, na.rm = TRUE)
sd_score    <- sd(scores, na.rm = TRUE)
range_score <- max(scores, na.rm = TRUE) - min(scores, na.rm = TRUE)
iq_range    <- IQR(scores, na.rm = TRUE)

summary_stats <- data.frame(
  Statistic = c("Mean", "Median", "Mode", "Variance", "Std Dev", "Range", "IQR"),
  Value = round(c(mean_score, median_score, mode_score, var_score, sd_score,
                  range_score, iq_range), 2)
)
summary_stats
```

The mean is `r round(mean_score, 1)` and the median is `r round(median_score, 1)`.
`r if (mean_score < median_score) "The mean sits below the median, which suggests a left (negative) skew pulled down by low scorers." else "The mean sits above the median, which suggests a right (positive) skew."`
The standard deviation of `r round(sd_score, 1)` marks a wide spread across the
class. The mode is a weak summary here because scores are continuous and few
values repeat.

## Extension: scores by pass/fail and gender

```{r groups}
aggregate(total_score ~ pass_fail, data = results,
          FUN = function(x) c(n = length(x), mean = round(mean(x), 1),
                              sd = round(sd(x), 1)))
aggregate(total_score ~ gender, data = results,
          FUN = function(x) c(n = length(x), mean = round(mean(x), 1),
                              sd = round(sd(x), 1)))
```

# Part 3: Distribution and normality

```{r histogram}
ggplot(results, aes(x = total_score)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "steelblue", color = "black", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean_score, color = "red", linetype = "dashed",
             linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median_score, color = "green", linetype = "dashed",
             linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Total Scores",
       subtitle = "Red = mean, green = median",
       x = "Total Score", y = "Frequency") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r qq}
qqnorm(scores)
qqline(scores, col = "red")
```

```{r shapiro}
shapiro_test <- shapiro.test(scores)
shapiro_test
```

The Shapiro-Wilk test gives W = `r round(shapiro_test$statistic, 3)` and
p = `r format(shapiro_test$p.value, digits = 3, scientific = TRUE)`.
`r if (shapiro_test$p.value < 0.05) "Because p < 0.05, we reject normality: the scores are not normally distributed. The histogram shows a cluster of very low scores (students who barely attended or sat the exam) alongside the main group, and the Q-Q plot departs from the line in the tails." else "Because p >= 0.05 we do not reject normality, and the Q-Q plot follows the line closely."`

## Scenario reasoning: which distribution fits?

* **Binomial:** A 10-question True/False quiz fits a binomial distribution
  because each question has two outcomes, there is a fixed number of trials
  (10), and the probability of success is constant per question.
* **Poisson:** Daily attendance counts fit a Poisson distribution if students
  arrive independently at a constant average rate.
* **Normal:** Total exam scores often approximate normality through the Central
  Limit Theorem, because many factors contribute and their sum tends toward a
  bell curve. This class does not follow that pattern perfectly (see the test
  above), mainly because of the students with near-zero totals.

# Part 4: One-sample hypothesis test

Test whether the class mean differs from a claimed value of 60.

* H0: mu = 60
* H1: mu != 60 (two-tailed), alpha = 0.05

```{r ttest}
t_test_result <- t.test(scores, mu = 60, alternative = "two.sided",
                        conf.level = 0.95)
t_test_result

t_statistic <- t_test_result$statistic
p_value     <- t_test_result$p.value
ci_lower    <- t_test_result$conf.int[1]
ci_upper    <- t_test_result$conf.int[2]

cat("Test Statistic (t):", round(t_statistic, 3), "\n")
cat("P-value:", signif(p_value, 4), "\n")
cat("95% Confidence Interval: [", round(ci_lower, 2), ",", round(ci_upper, 2), "]\n")
```

## Interpretation

We conducted a one-sample t-test to assess whether the class mean
(`r round(mean_score, 1)`) differs significantly from the claimed mean of 60.
The t-statistic is `r round(t_statistic, 2)` with p = `r signif(p_value, 3)`.
At the alpha = 0.05 level we
`r if (p_value < 0.05) "reject the null hypothesis" else "fail to reject the null hypothesis"`
(p `r if (p_value < 0.05) "<" else ">"` 0.05). The 95% confidence interval
[`r round(ci_lower, 1)`, `r round(ci_upper, 1)`]
`r if (ci_lower <= 60 && 60 <= ci_upper) "contains 60, so there is insufficient evidence that the true mean differs from 60." else "does not contain 60, so the true mean differs from 60."`
`r if (p_value < 0.05) "A Type I error is possible: we may have rejected a true null hypothesis, with probability at most 0.05." else "A Type II error is possible: our sample may have missed a real difference."`

Caveat: the t-test assumes approximately normal data. The Shapiro-Wilk result
above shows the scores are not perfectly normal, but with n =
`r length(scores)` the Central Limit Theorem makes the test of the mean
reasonably robust. As a non-parametric check I also ran a Wilcoxon signed-rank
test:

```{r wilcox}
wilcox_result <- wilcox.test(scores, mu = 60)
wilcox_result
```

The two tests give different answers (t-test p = `r signif(p_value, 3)`,
Wilcoxon p = `r signif(wilcox_result$p.value, 3)`). This is not a
contradiction: the t-test compares the **mean** to 60, and the mean
(`r round(mean_score, 1)`) is pulled down by the left skew, while the Wilcoxon
test compares the centre of the distribution, which is closer to the median
(`r round(median_score, 1)`), and that is near 60. So the evidence that the
typical student scores about 60 is fine, but the average is dragged below 60 by
the group of students with near-zero totals. The conclusion about the mean
should therefore be reported with this caveat.
